title: Purple Shine and the Unicorn Who Screams
subtitle: Book Five of the Castle Everstair stories

pages.spokenText: Purple Shine and the Unicorn Who Screams. Book Five of the Castle Everstair stories. Written with love by Luna and Sunny.

Everyone comes from a somewhere. It's true.
Cottontail sailed from an island of somewheres.
Winds slid down from a sky-colored one.
Even the sisters came out of the tower
(which counts, though nobody goes there on purpose).

But Moon and her sister were born with the moon —
zero years old, and they liked it that way —
and in four whole books, nobody asked,
not once, not even quietly:
born of whom?

One morning the sea made two circles of ripples,
and up the wet steps, dripping, came strangers:
a cat, purple all over, purple as plums,
and a dog, pink as morning, with sea in his fur.

Both had fairy wings, folded and fine.
Both had the tail of a mermaid. Both smiled.
"I'm Purple Shine," said the cat, with a bow.
"Pink Shine," woofed the dog.
And then, very strangely: "We're home."

Now, strangers know nothing. That's how strangers work.
But these two knew things there's no way to know.
They knew the twins' hide-spot (third stair from nowhere).
They knew Baby Lady takes tea with the honey
stirred nine times exactly — and never, never eight.

Winds gave them his carefullest, hugest sniff.
"They smell far," he said. "Not sea-far. Not sky-far.
A far I can't point at."
And Cottontail squinted her yellowest squint:
"Wings and a mermaid tail. Hmm.
Now where have I seen that recipe before?"

That night, Purple Shine forgot to be careful.
She hummed. Just a hum, soft and low in the lamplight.
And the hum was the twins' own lullaby. Theirs.
The one with the verse that they made up themselves —
the secret verse. Nobody knows it. Nobody.

She sang every word to the very last "sleep."
Then she saw the twins staring.
"...Lucky guess," said the cat.
And she looked at them long, and too soft, and away. … But the song always knows its way home.

Baby Lady heard it first. Her ears stood up.
A sound from the top of the top of all sounds,
so high that it hurt like a light in your eyes.

Out on the water, the waves pulled apart —
a road of bare seafloor from here to the dark —
and down that bare road came a clip and a clop.

And Purple Shine moved. Quick, like she'd practiced forever,
she stepped in front of the twins. Both of them.
Pink Shine stepped in front of her.

She was black. All-over black, like a hole in the night:
black coat and black mane and black spiraling horn,
with eyes like two coins of cold silver.
She never did say what her name was.
(Maybe she screamed it away, long ago.)

"Powers," she said, and her voice was a needle,
pitched higher than hearing would rather have gone.
"The moon-girl's. The pup's. Every shine in this castle.
Bring them to me — or I'll show you my scream."

Nobody brought her anything. So.

She planted four hooves, and she opened her mouth,
and the scream came out white — you could see it — in rings,
and the rings wanted things to be far from each other:
stones slid from stones; the foam flew off the sea.

And the rings caught the Shines like two kites with cut strings —
purple one way, pink the other — and gone.
Not hurt. Never hurt. Just away. So away
that no calling, no howling, no whistling could reach.

"Scream for them, then," said the unicorn, sweetly.
"Scream till your voices wear down to a whisper.
Nobody is coming for them.
And besides, little moonlings — you don't even know
who it is you've been losing, do you?

They came from tomorrow. They broke the way back.
It can't ever unclose. They knew, and they came.
Your mama. Your papa. They traded a world for you.
And now they are nowhere, calling your names —

and every power you have, handed to me,
is the price of your hearing them ever again."

And oh — it clicked, like a key in a lock.
The lullaby. The tea. The stepping-in-front.
The wings and the mermaid tail — Baby Lady's own recipe —
"I said that!" said Cottontail. "I said recipe!"

Moon sat down on the step. All the powers in the world,
and not one for a hole where your family was.
Her mama. Her papa. One evening of having them.

Then Baby Lady spoke, and she didn't speak big:
"We are zero years old. We are brand new at this.
But nobody loses our parents on birthday-week.
Up, sister. We're going to go find them." … But the song always knows its way home.

But how do you find what you cannot hear?
You sing. You sing what your family sings.

So the twins stood together on the very bottom step,
and they sang the secret verse of their lullaby
out into all of the quiet at once.

And far in one faraway, something purple stopped crying.
And far in another, something pink raised his ears.
And between four hearts — daughter, daughter, mama, papa —
a thread pulled tight.
And the thread began to glow.

Moon's thread ran to Purple Shine; down it came everything —
all that her mama was, meeting all that Moon was.
And Baby Lady's ran to Pink Shine, just the same.
And pop — on each twin's head — a crown. A purple crown.

And gold poured over them, wingtip to tail-tip:
gold wings! Gold tails! Every feather, every scale —
everything gold but their necklaces,
which stayed exactly as they were.
(Some things are already exactly right.)

And the world went loud with family. They could hear.
A purple hum, west. A woolly bark, east.
They flew, and they found, and they fell on their parents —
the first hug that knew what a hug it was.

Crowns can't fight, you know.
But crowns can find.

"How sweet," said the voice from the top of all voices.
"Found each other. Then I'll scream you apart again —
farther this time. Forever this time —
unless somebody hands me those powers."

And she opened her mouth, and the white rings came
bigger than ever, and even the crowns
dug in like anchors, and started to slide.

Because here's what a scream like that needs, to win.
Two things. Only two.
Everyone apart. Everyone quiet. … But the song always knows its way home.

And nobody planned what came next. That's the good part.

Cottontail came claws-first, hollering.
Winds surfed in riding a shout of a wind.
Evilest stomped up, already yelling,
Cheeblest came running, bows coming loose,
and Beedlist came quietly, book to her chest.

And the parents and twins stood up in the middle,
and everyone grabbed onto everyone else.

"Apart isn't working," said Moon, "exactly."
"So," said her sister. "Nobody be that."

It was Pink Shine who started it — one woolly note —
and the lullaby rose with everybody in it:
Moon high and clear, and her sister beneath her,
the jaguars roaring it, wildly off-key
(off-key doesn't matter; together does),
Evilest belting, Cheeblest sweet,
and Beedlist — Beedlist held her book open
to the words, and mouthed every single one.

Then a voice joined in, soft as snowfall,
from somewhere behind. And nobody turned.
And one more voice, high and small,
from nowhere that anyone looked.

And the scream hit the song, and could not get in.
A scream needs a quiet to tear at. An apart.
And there wasn't any. There wasn't any at all.

The scream went thin. Then the scream went thread.
Then the scream was a kettle, far off. Then nothing.
And the unicorn stood in the nothing she'd made,
black as a hole in the night. But smaller.

"You could sing too," offered Moon. "There's room.
There's always room in a song this size."

The unicorn looked a long look at them all —
at everyone holding on to everyone.
Then she turned down the bare sea road, and was gone,
and the water closed gently behind her.

And far, far out, where the dark begins:
one note. Hummed. Badly.
Just one.

The birthday came two mornings later.
One birthday, two twins — that's the deal with twins —
and they turned zero again, the way that they do,
and nobody questioned the math.

(The purple crowns had gone when the singing was done —
finding-crowns do that — and that was all right.)

The whole of everybody came. The table groaned.
(Somebody drank from the stormy bowl early.
Nobody minded at all.)

"Our world is gone," said Purple Shine, softly.
"This one has soup," said Baby Lady. "And us."

And when it was time for the birthday song,
two voices sang loudest of all — their first birthday
of being right there. And the song, as you know —
as you knew all along —
was the same song that won. … But the song always knows its way home.
